note: Addresses the common client case of using pretrained or off the shelf models, and ties actions to ISO 27090 and OWASP.
title: Compliance Made Practical: Translating the EU AI Act into Implementable Security Actions
journal: IEEE/ACM International Workshop on Responsible AI Engineering
explain_beginner: The EU AI Act requires AI systems to be secure, but most companies today do not build their AI models from scratch, they take an existing pretrained model and adapt it, which raises a specific practical question this paper tackles, whose job is it to secure a system built on someone else's model, and what exactly do they need to do. The paper looks at the technical guidance that already exists, official reports from ISO and Europe's cybersecurity agency ENISA that describe AI security risks thoroughly but read more like textbooks than checklists, and contrasts them with industry resources like OWASP's AI security guides, which are more hands on but were not written with the AI Act's specific legal requirements in mind. The author's contribution is connecting these two worlds specifically for the pretrained model scenario, translating the law's general security mandate into concrete actions, tied to a data security standard for AI that was still being finalized at the time.
explain_business: Most organizations deploying AI today are exactly the audience this paper targets, teams using a vendor's foundation model, an open weights model, or an API rather than training from scratch, and the practical message is that AI Act security compliance still applies to them even though they did not build the underlying model, with responsibility landing on how the model is deployed, configured, and monitored rather than on how it was originally trained. The actionable path the paper offers is to use OWASP's AI Exchange and LLM Top 10 as the practical checklist and treat the ISO/IEC technical reports as the underlying risk rationale regulators will expect referenced. Because part of this guidance was tied to ISO/IEC 27090 before that standard was finalized, teams building a compliance program around it now should confirm they are working from the standard's final published version rather than the draft state this paper described.
explain_practitioner: Bunzel's paper addresses AI Act security compliance specifically for the common case of organizations deploying pretrained or off the shelf models rather than training their own, arguing that existing technical guidance, ISO/IEC technical reports 24028 and 24029 and ENISA's Securing Machine Learning Algorithms report, comprehensively covers relevant risks and mitigations but lacks actionable, hands on implementation steps. The paper positions OWASP's AI Exchange and OWASP LLM Top 10 as filling that practical gap, and its contribution is mapping AI Act security obligations onto concrete actions organizations can take when they do not control the base model, tied specifically to the then upcoming ISO/IEC 27090 standard. As a synthesis and mapping paper rather than an empirical study, it reports no test results or dataset, and its clearest limitation is timing, part of its practical guidance is anchored to ISO/IEC 27090 while that standard was still being finalized, meaning organizations following it needed to track the standard's final text rather than treating the paper's mapping as permanently fixed.
